entry.title: What does Mossberry do in Hollow Knight: Silksong?
entry.summary:
As a cryptic metroidvania, Hollow Knight: Silksong often gives you items you have no idea what to do with. It's the usual Soulslike formula: piece things together yourself.
In one of the early stages of the game, you'll uncover an item called Mossberry, which you'll probably be puzzled about. Its purpose is actually pretty simple, though, so here's everything you need to know.
What is Mossberry in Hollow Knight: Silksong?
The Mossberry item can be found around the Mosshome zone. Screenshot by Destructoid
Mossberries are a quest item found in the game's initial area, the Mosshome. They are green bulbous orbs often carried by other bugs, which you have to defeat to acquire. They are tied to a particular character in Mosshome, the Moss Druid. She can be found by accessing the area past the Map Merchant in The Marrow, particularly its right side.
Once you've reached the Moss Druid, she will offer you a Berry Picking quest, which you have to Promise to fulfill. You then have to collect three of these Mossberries and bring them back to her, which will give you a reward.
This quest is entirely optional and can take a while, given how scattered the Mossberry enemies are throughout the Mosshome zone. We're crafting a dedicated guide regarding this assignment, so make sure to keep an eye out for that.

entry.title: Should you insert 30 Rosaries in Hollow Knight: Silksong?
entry.summary:
Hollow Knight: Silksong is out, and you just know it has a ton of secrets and strange choices you can make. One of them is found quite early in the game, asking you to spend 30 hard-earned Rosaries without knowing what will happen.
But we're here to help demystify this choice and ensure you made the right decision.
“Insert Rosaries” in Hollow Knight: Silksong, explained
The bell asks you to spend 30 hard-earned Rosaries without knowing what'll happen. Screenshot by Destructoid
During one of the earliest stages of the game, just after you've passed the first shop and village, you'll walk into a strange bell contraption. Going near it prompts you to interact with it, and then asks you to spend 30 Rosaries without revealing what will happen.
Rosaries are the primary currency in shops and other locations in Hollow Knight: Silksong and are quite valuable, so spending 30 of your first ones is a tough choice. However, pressing "Yes" here rewards you with a Rest spot, i.e., a bonfire, meaning you get a checkpoint for the low, low price of 30 Rosaries.
Thus, I think you should go for "Yes" here, since having an extra starting point to explore from is always welcome and will spare you the significant backtracking you'd have to do otherwise (given your last rest spot was way back in the village).

entry.title: How to save your game in Hollow Knight: Silksong
entry.summary:
It's easy to miss the save spot in Hollow Knight: Silksong. While the game shows you an icon when it's saving, it may still not help you find exactly when and how to save your progress.
You can save in Silksong by pressing up next to a rest bench. This bench looks like a small altar with a backrest made of shells (that actually look like bones), and it will show a balloon with "Rest" on top of it when you approach it. When you press up next to the bench, Hornet will sit, and you'll see the save icon pop up on the bottom right of your screen and hear a high-pitched chime at the same time. You'll also recover Hornet's health.
Rest and save all at once. Screenshot by Destructoid.
All that happens pretty quickly and without any prompt like "Would you like to save your game?", which is why it's easy to miss and think you haven't saved it. If for any reason you want to heal but don't want to save on a certain spot, you can't. You'll heal and save at once whenever you sit on a bench.
The first save bench in Silksong is to the left of the area that triggers Hornet feeling unwell for the second time. Just keep walking to the left, and you'll see a bright area with the bench.

Damian Poddebniak, Christian Dresen, Jens Müller, Fabian Ising, Sebastian Schinzel, Simon Friedberger, Juraj Somorovsky, and Jörg Schwenk discovered that KMail could be made to leak the plaintext of S/MIME encrypted emails when retrieving external content in emails. entry.title: What can a 34-year-old Sonic level teach us about videogame light?
entry.summary:
No videogame fantasy setting will ever disquiet me as much as an empty business park at night under blue and yellow floodlights. A business park, or the access road down the side of a corrugated steel warehouse, where the alcoves cast by the LEDs look like a procession of hooded figures beneath the fixed, unblinking blackness of the sky. I can't actually be present in that scene, mind. I don't belong there. No being does, not even the people who come by day to fill the striped lines with cars or raise the shutters on the loading bays. Instead, I have to be travelling past very fast. Preferably, I will be looking out the window of a train that shows the place for only a few seconds. I will feel as though I've glimpsed another planet's scrolling surface in a mirror. Except this isn't right. I will never find the words for it. Nothing written above is adequate. Balls.

entry.title: Bunnyhop elsewhere, streamers: EA are making Battlefield 6 more strategic, less run-and-gun following the beta
entry.summary:
The Battlefield 6 beta is officially a Thing That Happened, and now comes the terrible ordeal of Learning From The Experience. Here is what developers DICE, Criterion, Motive and Ripple Effect have learned from the experience: you are all playing the game far too much like Call Of Duty. Goodness me, it's like 2007 never ended. Doing headshots in midair? That's an updatin'. Doing a parkour while carrying a light machinegun? That's an updatin'. Bunny-hopping with prejudice? You'd best believe that's an updatin'. Never mind that those multiplayer reveal montages emphasised footloose quickdraw almost as much as they incited a murderous contempt for helicopters. It's time to play Battlefield the way Battlefield should be played: lying in a hole praying that one of your team-mates spawns on you before a tank rolls over your head.

entry.title: Lithuanian Regulator Clashes With Data Firm Over “Misleading” Piracy Stats
entry.summary: Lithuania's broadcasting regulator (LRTK) challenges the accuracy of data reported by piracy tracking firm MUSO, which is the main input for key EUIPO reports. Citing flaws such as the inclusion of legal sites and an inability to track VPN or IPTV use, LRTK argues that its country is being unfairly portrayed as a piracy leader. In response, MUSO says the LRTK's statements are themselves misleading and the company demands a correction. From: TF, for the latest news on copyright battles, piracy and more.

entry.title: The first hours of Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines 2 uncloak a slick action game, but a limited RPG
entry.summary: I feel for Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines 2. If it was named something like Fang Bastard: The Punching Of The Many, the trailers wouldn’t have so many views, but those who’d watched them would probably be quite jazzed for that new bitey-talky game that looks a bit like Dishonored with more story branching. It isn’t, and they aren’t. Instead, it’s called Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines 2, a name packed with some of the weightiest words in RPGdom. I don’t pity it, though. Three hours and change into Bloodlines 2, I’ve determined that I’d quite enjoy a Dishonored with more story branching, actually. Not as much as if I could express my roleplaying chops outside of very specific dialogue menus, or if I cared more about the fellow nightcrawlers on the other side of those conversations. But for all the tricky development and heavy heritage, I’d be lying if I said I haven’t enjoyed being The Chinese Room’s version of a souped-up vampire prowling a snowy, bisexual-lit Seattle.
